title: NURS 1017 Unit 6 Case Study 2

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.
question.explanation:
Require immediate follow-up:

Shortened, externally rotated, deformed right leg: the classic picture of a displaced femoral shaft fracture. The limb must be immobilized (splinted or in traction) before any movement, and neurovascular status is checked often.

Tachycardia (116 beats/min), BP 100/62 mm Hg, and pale, cool, diaphoretic skin: a closed femoral shaft fracture can hide 1 to 1.5 L of blood in the thigh. These are early signs of hypovolemic shock and must be reported now.

Squared-off shoulder that he cannot move: the humeral head has left the joint (anterior dislocation is the most common type). A dislocation is reduced as soon as possible to protect the nerves, blood vessels and joint cartilage.

Numbness over the outer upper arm: the axillary nerve wraps around the neck of the humerus and is the nerve most often injured by an anterior shoulder dislocation. Sensation is documented before and after reduction.

Do not need immediate follow-up: intact skin over the fracture (a closed fracture), a warm, pink foot with strong pulses and brisk capillary refill, a strong left radial pulse, a temperature of 36.6° C, SpO₂ 97% and an RR of 22 breaths/min (expected with pain). The abrasions need cleaning but are not urgent.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 22-year-old male client brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle collision.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is consistent with a fracture, a dislocation, or a subluxation.

rows.text: Humeral head lying completely outside the glenoid cavity on X-ray
Shortening and external rotation of the leg
Shoulder that “popped partly out” and slid back in on its own
Bone broken into several fragments on X-ray
Partial loss of contact between the joint surfaces, which remain partly aligned
Squared-off shoulder contour with loss of normal movement

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1620 and the Diagnostic Results.
question.explanation:
Fracture: a break in the continuity of a bone. This client's femur fracture is closed (skin intact) and comminuted (more than two fragments). Other types: open (bone ends break through the skin), transverse (straight across), oblique (at an angle), spiral (twisting around the shaft from a rotational force), greenstick (incomplete, on one side of a bendable child's bone), compression (bone crushed, as in vertebrae), impacted (one fragment driven into another), avulsion (a fragment pulled off by a tendon or ligament) and pathologic (through bone weakened by disease). Muscle spasm pulls the overriding femur fragments together, shortening and rotating the leg.

Dislocation: the joint surfaces lose contact completely, as the X-ray shows for the left shoulder. The joint looks deformed (the shoulder is squared off because the humeral head no longer fills out the deltoid) and cannot move normally.

Subluxation: a partial dislocation; the joint surfaces still touch in part. It often reduces on its own, as in his hockey injuries. Repeated subluxations stretch the capsule and ligaments, which made this full dislocation more likely.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client is most likely experiencing [[drop0]] as evidenced by [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is the client's [[drop2]].

alcohol withdrawal
compartment syndrome
fat embolism syndrome
a temperature of 38.4° C

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 2100 and Day 3 0300, the Vital Signs from Day 3 0300, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Fat embolism syndrome (FES) occurs most often 24 to 72 hours after a fracture of a long bone (especially the femur) or the pelvis, or after surgery on the marrow canal. Fat globules from the marrow enter torn veins and lodge in the lungs, brain and skin. Free fatty acids released from the fat damage the capillaries, causing inflammation and leaky lung capillaries.

The classic triad: respiratory distress with hypoxemia (SpO₂ 86%, PO₂ 54 mm Hg, with a low PCO₂ from rapid breathing), neurologic changes (restlessness, confusion) and petechiae on the chest, axillae and conjunctivae, which usually appear last. Fever, tachycardia, a falling platelet count and anemia support the diagnosis.

Why not the others: compartment syndrome causes severe pain and neurovascular changes in the limb, but his foot is warm with strong pulses and his pain is 4/10. His blood pressure is stable, so this is not hypovolemic shock; some fall in hemoglobin after surgery is expected. Alcohol withdrawal can cause confusion but not hypoxemia and petechiae. Fever and the hemoglobin value alone do not point to a cause.

Priority: airway and breathing come first. The client's oxygenation is failing (impaired gas exchange), which also explains his confusion. Pain, infection risk and mobility matter but are not life-threatening now.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 22-year-old male client brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle collision.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take at this time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply oxygen according to the unit's protocol and monitor SpO₂ continuously
Handle the right leg as little as possible and keep it supported in alignment
Stay with the client and call the rapid response team
Recheck the vital signs at the next scheduled time, 0400
Lower the head of the bed and raise the legs
Offer cold oral fluids to bring down the fever
Reassess level of consciousness and breathing frequently
Raise the head of the bed
Help the client walk to the bathroom to expand his lungs
Massage the right calf to improve circulation

question.explanation:
Correct: the client's oxygenation and level of consciousness are deteriorating, so the nurse stays with him and calls the rapid response team. Raising the head of the bed improves lung expansion and oxygenation. Oxygen is started under the unit's protocol, with continuous pulse oximetry. Frequent reassessment shows whether he is improving or needs airway support. Moving the fractured limb as little as possible limits further release of fat from the marrow.

Incorrect: massaging the calf could dislodge a clot if a deep vein thrombosis is present and does nothing for the lungs. Lowering the head of the bed worsens breathing. A confused, hypoxemic client with a newly repaired femur must not walk. Oral fluids risk aspiration in a confused, breathless client. Waiting for the next scheduled check delays care while he deteriorates.

question.stem: The nurse uses the client's question to teach him how a fracture heals. Place the stages of bone healing in order, from the first stage to the last.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 6 1000 and the Vital Signs from Day 6 1000.
question.explanation:
1. Hematoma formation (first days): torn blood vessels bleed into the fracture site and a clot forms. Inflammatory cells clear debris, and the clot becomes the framework for repair.

2. Cellular proliferation (about days 3 to 14): capillaries, fibroblasts and osteoblasts invade the clot, turning it into granulation tissue.

3. Callus formation (weeks 2 to 6): cartilage and woven bone form a callus around and between the bone ends. The fracture is held together but is not yet strong, which is why weight bearing is limited.

4. Ossification (weeks 3 to 12 or more): minerals are laid down and the callus becomes hard bone. On X-ray, bridging bone crosses the fracture line.

5. Remodeling (months to a year or more): osteoclasts remove the excess callus and the bone is reshaped along the lines of stress, restoring near-normal strength.

Healing times vary with the bone, the age of the client, the blood supply and other factors. A large weight-bearing bone such as the femur typically takes several months to unite. Smoking, poor nutrition, low vitamin D, infection, diabetes, corticosteroids and movement at the fracture site all slow healing.
orderedOptions: Hematoma formation: bleeding at the fracture forms a clot between the bone ends, and inflammation begins
Cellular proliferation: new capillaries, fibroblasts and bone-forming cells grow into the clot, forming granulation tissue
Callus formation: cartilage and immature (woven) bone form a soft callus that bridges the fracture
Ossification: the callus is mineralized into hard bone, uniting the fragments
Remodeling: osteoclasts remove excess callus and the bone regains its shape and strength

question.stem: For each finding at the 6-month visit, click to specify whether it shows that an expected outcome has been met or that it requires follow-up.

rows.text: Fracture line still visible, with callus that does not bridge the fracture
Full range of motion of the left shoulder with no further dislocations
Normal sensation over the outer left upper arm
Aching at the fracture site with full weight bearing, managed with ibuprofen most days
Right foot warm with pedal pulses 2+ and no calf swelling

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 180 1000, the Diagnostic Results from Day 180, the Vital Signs from Day 180, and the Laboratory Results from Day 180.
question.explanation:
Expected outcomes met: the shoulder has healed without recurrence and the axillary nerve has recovered. Circulation to the right leg is normal with no signs of deep vein thrombosis. The hemoglobin has returned to normal after the blood loss.

Requires follow-up: delayed union. By 6 months a femur would be expected to show bridging bone. A fracture that heals more slowly than expected is a delayed union; if healing stops altogether it becomes a nonunion; a fracture that heals in a poor position is a malunion. Pain at the fracture site with weight bearing is a sign that the bone has not united.

Factors slowing his healing, which the nurse reports and addresses: smoking (nicotine constricts blood vessels and reduces oxygen delivery to the healing bone); low vitamin D (needed to absorb calcium for mineralizing the callus); and regular NSAID use (evidence suggests NSAIDs may interfere with the inflammatory phase of bone healing). The nurse reports these findings to the provider, offers smoking cessation support, and reinforces nutrition with enough protein, calcium and vitamin D.

description: 22-year-old male client after a motorcycle collision with a closed comminuted femur fracture and an anterior shoulder dislocation (after earlier subluxations); fracture types, dislocation vs subluxation, fat embolism syndrome on Day 3, the five stages of bone healing, and delayed union at 6 months.

authorReview.note:
New case written by Claude on 14 Oct 2026 to fill a Unit 6 gap; please review before using it with students:
Screen 5: the five stages of bone healing are worded hematoma, cellular proliferation, callus, ossification, remodeling; match your textbook's names.
Screen 6: the NSAID effect on bone healing is described as possible (the evidence is mixed); timing of delayed union for the femur (no bridging at 6 months) should suit your teaching.
Screen 3: timing of fat embolism (about 36 hours after injury) and the ABG values are illustrative.
